description: Our team is building a mission planner for the Moon’s south pole using real NASA lunar data. It ranks landing sites by safety, sunlight, and access to water ice, and shows them on a 3D map with a simulated landing and rover route. We chose this challenge because it has the best data, a strong visual demo, and a direct connection to NASA’s Artemis missions.
summary:
Lunar Lookout is a tool to help plan lunar landing sites. Due to the low Sun angle near the south pole a lander can spend weeks in darkness whilst the ridge can block the Earth, causing loss in communications. By choosing a landing location and date you will be able to determine when your lander will get sunlight and good visibility.

Using accurate NASA LRO LOLA data this calculates the true local horizon for each site. This works on NASA’s 9 Artemis landing candidates, other landing sites or custom coordinates. It will score each site on survivability (power), communications and visibility. A result of GO, CAUTION or NO-GO will be provided. This can be compared for up to 5 locations. See how delays affect the landing site. Get the best landing date in the next 60 days. With 3D terrain visuals and a light map.

Sun and Earth positions are verified live using JPL Horizons with an accuracy of 0.003°. Verified with published studies and NASA’s illumination maps.
details:
What it does and how it works
Lunar Lookout helps mission planners, teachers and the public judge a Moon landing site by its sunlight and its line of sight to Earth. You choose a site and a landing date, then pick a mission length of 14 to 90 days. The app computes where the Sun and Earth sit above the local horizon hour by hour. It uses the real terrain horizon from NASA’s LRO LOLA elevation model (3812 × 3812 heights at 240 m per pixel), loaded in the browser. From that it reports:

  • the share of the mission in sunlight, and the longest night
  • the share of time Earth is in view, and the longest blackout
  • the lowest battery level, from a simple power model (450 W array, 120 W draw, 8.6 kWh battery)
  • an overall Landing Site Score and a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO call

It also compares up to five sites side by side, shows what a launch slip of one day to one month does, and scans the next 60 days to find the best landing day at NASA’s Artemis regions. A 3D terrain view, a south pole lighting map, and an AI mission advisor chatbot help explain the results.

Why it matters
Planning tools for this exist, but their interfaces are hard to use. Lunar Lookout puts the answer in one screen, with a plain-language forecast (“Sunny, sunset in 106.5 days · Earth below the horizon, Earthrise in 8.8 h”).

How we know it’s right
Every time the page loads, it runs a check against NASA JPL Horizons. Sun and Earth positions agree to within 0.003°. The app also reproduces NASA’s 18.6-year illumination averages at 15 sites. It matches published values for Shackleton crater depth, Malapert Massif height, permanently shadowed floors, and the connecting ridge’s sunlight and longest night. The source code includes tests that reproduce these numbers.

Tools used
TypeScript and JavaScript, Astronomy Engine, three.js, esbuild (single-file build), and the Google Gemini API for the chatbot. We used Claude by Anthropic as an AI assistant to help build and test the project.

Limits
“Earth in view” means a clear line of sight, not a full radio link budget. Results are planning estimates, not certified landing safety assessments.
